title: IBM: Three Demonstrations Prove Quantum Advantage Has Been Reached
gist: IBM and partners Algorithmiq, Qedma and University of Chicago researchers published three demonstrations on IBM's Heron chips that they say meet IBM's own quantum-advantage requirements: results more accurate and cheaper than classical methods and rigorously validatable. The hardest number is Qedma's 700,000 Fugaku CPU hours failing to match what Heron r3 produced in seven hours, backed by cross-checks on Quantinuum trapped-ion machines and a spacetime-code replacement for random circuit sampling aimed at the verification problem.

themes.theme: Where the advantage bar actually sits

insights.claim: Quantum advantage requires solving a practical, real-world problem more quickly, cheaply or accurately than a classical supercomputer, whereas quantum supremacy only requires beating classical machines at any task even if the job itself is useless - the usefulness of the problem is the dividing line.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This distinction is the filter for judging every vendor claim in the sector.
insights.quote: The usefulness of the problem solved is the difference between advantage and supremacy.
insights.locator: There are slight differences in the definition

insights.claim: Every prior headline claim in quantum has been contested - Google's Echoes Algorithm on the Willow chip, Q-CTRL's May materials-science claim run on IBM's Quantum Platform, Google's 2019 53-qubit Sycamore supremacy result and D-Wave's Advantage 2 annealing claim - leaving the scientific community still debating whether advantage has been reached.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Claim inflation is the norm here; discount announcements that lack independent validation.
insights.locator: Some vendors have claimed to have reached quantum advantage

insights.claim: IBM defining advantage requirements jointly with Pasqal and running a platform-agnostic Quantum Advantage Tracker positions it as referee of the whole field's claims rather than merely another claimant.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Owning the validation framework is a moat that outlasts any single hardware generation.
insights.locator: IBM and quantum startup Pasqal last year laid out

insights.claim: IBM Research director Jay Gambetta frames the milestone as trust and validation rather than raw computational power, arguing results can now be verified with confidence even for problems classical methods cannot solve.
insights.speaker: Jay Gambetta
insights.so_what: Verifiability, not qubit count, is the metric IBM wants the market to price.
insights.quote: These demonstrations prove that we can scale quantum computing forward with confidence,
insights.locator: It’s an important step on the continuing trek

insights.claim: Algorithmiq's simulation of real-world disordered matter has stood on the Quantum Advantage Tracker for eight months with no classical system reliably reproducing its results at scale, after IBM reran it on other quantum processors with different noise and calibrations and classical-simulation partners including the Flatiron Institute tried to break it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: An eight-month unbroken claim is the strongest durability evidence yet offered for a quantum advantage result.
insights.locator: In the eight months since it was pulled into the Quantum Advantage Tracker

insights.claim: Two different IBM quantum chips produced results consistent within the margin of error every time, while classical simulation methods pushed to their memory and time limits could not match the quantum results and did not even agree with each other.
insights.speaker: Sabrina Maniscalco
insights.so_what: Disagreement among classical baselines is being used as affirmative evidence - a new and contestable standard of proof.
insights.quote: They didn't even agree with each other,
insights.locator: The experiments using two different IBM quantum chips

insights.claim: The commercially relevant target for early quantum simulation is messy matter - catalysts and battery electrolytes with irregular structures - precisely because the disorder that makes these materials useful for clean energy is what makes them hard to simulate classically.
insights.speaker: Sabrina Maniscalco
insights.so_what: Points the first quantum revenue pools at energy-materials R&D rather than finance or logistics optimization.
insights.quote: All materials that will power the next generation of clean energy and industry are messy, disordered, and irregular, and this messiness is exactly what makes them hard to simulate, and exactly why understanding the matters.
insights.locator: Most of the physics that we are taught in school

insights.claim: Qedma's QESEM error suppression and mitigation software let a 51-bit IBM system resolve oscillations in laser-driven materials, run first without the software, then in a mode with a theoretical guarantee of convergence, then in a more efficient variant that drops the guarantee to push further.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Error-mitigation software is emerging as a separately monetizable layer between quantum hardware and applications.
insights.locator: Qedma ran simulations using a 51-bit IBM system

insights.claim: The classical baseline broke down early: finite-size scaling on Fugaku with 28- and 35-electron models saw the time and magnetization simulations diverge, and the H100 server ran out of memory and produced bad results, while real-sized materials involve billions of electrons.
insights.speaker: Netanel Linder
insights.so_what: The classical extrapolation ladder fails well below industrially relevant system sizes.
insights.quote: Actually, the H100 server runs out of memory and starts getting really bad results,
insights.locator: The researchers initially ran it on the Fugaku supercomputer

insights.claim: Qedma burned 700,000 CPU hours on Fugaku without reproducing the oscillations that IBM Heron r3 'Boston' systems produced in seven hours, and closing the gap classically would require roughly 80,000 GPU servers running for half a year.
insights.speaker: Netanel Linder
insights.so_what: The first hard cost-of-compute comparison an investor can underwrite: seven quantum hours against an infeasible classical bill.
insights.locator: QEDMA ran Fugaku for 700,000 CPU hours

insights.claim: Validation ran across modalities: the same results were reproduced on Quantinuum's H2 and Helios trapped-ion machines, a different modality from IBM's superconducting systems, before scaling to two 74-qubit systems representing materials with billions of electrons.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Cross-modality reproduction is becoming the de facto validation standard, favoring vendors with partner access.
insights.locator: To validate the results, Qedma ran the tests on two quantum models from Quantinuum

insights.claim: Qedma claims this is the first quantum advantage experiment run on commercially available hardware using commercially available software, making error reduction the unlock for trusted quantum performance.
insights.speaker: Netanel Linder
insights.so_what: Shifts the story from lab demo to purchasable stack - the precondition for a real quantum services market.
insights.quote: In the end, this is the first quantum advantage experiment that was done on commercially available hardware using commercially available software,
insights.locator: In the end, this is the first quantum advantage experiment

themes.theme: Verifiable replacement for random circuit sampling

insights.claim: University of Chicago researchers working with IBM built a structured alternative to random circuit sampling using spacetime codes - an extremely complex circuit into which insular qubits are injected, symmetries measured and results filtered into an error-correction code - to attack the verification problem that makes such results unprovable without assumptions about the device.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Verification is the bottleneck that kept prior supremacy claims from being bankable; this is the attempt to remove it.
insights.locator: University of Chicago researchers created a structured alternative

insights.claim: The demonstration ran about 70 logical qubits using about 21 insulars with up to 2,415 logical two-qubit gates plus 468 logical T gates, cut effective device error by a factor of ten, and completed in about 16 minutes versus much longer classical simulation times.
insights.speaker: Jay Gambetta
insights.so_what: Concrete logical-qubit and gate-depth numbers to benchmark the next generation of hardware claims against.
insights.quote: This allows us to run on about 70 logical qubits using about 21 insulars and run up to 2,415 logical two-qubit gates,
insights.locator: Researchers have been working on spacetime codes

insights.claim: Adding T gates up to 75 left the properties of the error-correcting code unchanged, letting researchers dial up the classical simulation complexity while keeping error correction intact and preserving the complexity separation.
insights.speaker: Jay Gambetta
insights.so_what: A knob that raises the classical hardness of the benchmark without degrading fidelity - the core of the verifiable-advantage argument.
insights.quote: As we add more T gates, we do not see any properties of the error correction code changing,
insights.locator: They verified the simulation by adding more T gates
